vignette:
Minh was fifty years old, a guitarist who had spent thirty years playing in bars and small venues across the Bay Area, before the stalking began. It started with a woman who appeared at three consecutive shows, always standing at the same spot near the stage left, her eyes fixed on him with an intensity that felt like a physical pressure. He ignored it at first, the way musicians learn to ignore the strange energies that drift up from the crowd. But then she began waiting outside the back door after gigs, and once, he found a note tucked under the windshield wiper of his van that read simply, I see you when you don't see me. The police told him there was nothing they could do until she made a direct threat, and the sense of institutional failure — the feeling that the people who should have protected him had simply shrugged — settled into him like a splinter he could not remove. He changed his routine, stopped playing late shows, and eventually moved apartments, but the memory of those months had already carved itself into him in a way that felt broken.

What Minh could not escape was the way the memory came back: not as a story he told himself, but as sudden pieces — the smell of the alley behind the venue, the sound of her heels on the pavement, the shape of her silhouette against the streetlight — that appeared without warning and then vanished, leaving him disoriented and cold. When these fragments hit, they felt completely real across all his senses at once, as though he had been dropped back into that moment. There were also gaps: entire stretches of those weeks that he could not retrieve no matter how hard he tried, and the fact that his own mind had erased parts of his life made him feel weak, as though he had not been strong enough to hold onto himself. He had come to believe that he was a weak person, that a stronger man would have confronted her, would have handled it without falling apart. That belief hollowed him out. He felt dead inside, emotionally numb, and he was certain that this numbness was just further proof of his failure — that a real person would still feel something, would still care.

The numbness made it harder to remember the details clearly, as though his mind had decided that if he was not going to feel the fear properly, it would not give him the full picture. And then the gaps in his memory, in turn, reinforced his sense of weakness: if he could not even remember what had happened, how could he trust himself to handle anything? This loop tightened over the months that followed. Every time a fragment of the memory surfaced — the sound of her voice, the way she had smiled — his threat system would spike, and he would start watching other people closely, scanning their faces for signs that they might harm him. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely, because he could not assess the danger in them, and he found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, so he stopped leaving his apartment after sunset. This meant he could no longer take gigs that ended late, which was most of them. His income dropped. His bandmates grew frustrated. He stopped returning their calls.

The threat monitoring made the memory fragments come more frequently — the more he watched others, the more his brain seemed to find matches for the danger it was looking for, and each match triggered another flash of sensory reliving. Each flash, in turn, deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally broken, that a normal person would have moved on by now. He had become a man who spent his days in a single room, checking the locks twice before dark, his guitar case gathering dust in the corner. What finally brought him to seek help was not the fear itself, but the silence: three weeks since anyone had called him, and he had realized he could not remember the last time he had played a note. He was terrified that the music was gone, and he was even more terrified that he had been the one to kill it.
